title: Yarn weight system
subtitle: From 4-ply to chunky — what the weights mean and how to substitute
excerpt: Yarn weights name the thickness of a yarn. From lace and 4-ply at the fine end to chunky and super chunky at the heavy end. The right weight matters more than the brand or fibre — substitute within the weight and the pattern still works.
sourceNotes: Modern Craft Yarn Council standard yarn-weight system. British yarn-weight history from late-Victorian Weldon's Practical Crochet through to mid-twentieth-century Patons and Sirdar pattern leaflets.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wraps per inch. A measurement of yarn thickness — wrap the yarn around a ruler and count how many wraps fit in a 2.5 cm space. Useful for identifying an unlabelled yarn.

heroPrompt: Five balls of yarn arranged in a row on a pale background, from finest (lace) on the left to chunkiest on the right, each in plain cream — the thickness difference is clearly visible.

content.text: Yarn weights name the thickness of a yarn. A pattern asks for a specific weight; you can substitute any yarn of the same weight and the pattern still works. The fibre type changes the drape and warmth; the brand changes price and feel; but the weight controls the size of the stitches.
British and American conventions name the weights differently. The translation table below covers the seven standard weights.
The seven standard weights
Lace (UK: 2-ply, US: lace). The finest. About 0.5 mm thick. Used for crochet lace and fine doilies. Hook size 1.5-2.5 mm.
Fingering (UK: 4-ply, US: fingering). About 0.8 mm. Used for fine cardigans, baby clothes, socks. Hook size 2.5-3.5 mm.
Sport (UK: 5-ply, US: sport). About 1 mm. Used for fine adult garments and lightweight blankets. Hook size 3.5-4 mm.
DK (UK: DK or double knitting, US: light worsted). About 1.5 mm. The most-used British yarn weight. Used for everything from blankets and garments to amigurumi. Hook size 4-4.5 mm.
Aran (UK: aran, US: worsted). About 2 mm. Used for sweaters, hats, mittens, throws. Hook size 5-5.5 mm.
Chunky (UK: chunky, US: bulky). About 2.5-3 mm. Used for quick blankets, winter jumpers, scarves. Hook size 6-8 mm.
Super chunky (UK: super chunky, US: super bulky). 3 mm and up. Used for the fastest projects — chunky throws, hot-water-bottle covers, statement scarves. Hook size 9-15 mm.
Identifying an unlabelled yarn
For stash balls without labels, use the
WPI
test — wraps per inch. Wrap the yarn around a ruler with each wrap touching the next, and count how many wraps fit in 2.5 cm (1 inch):
Lace: 35 or more wraps per inch.
Fingering / 4-ply: 19-22 wraps.
Sport / 5-ply: 15-18 wraps.
DK: 11-14 wraps.
Aran / worsted: 9-11 wraps.
Chunky / bulky: 7-9 wraps.
Super chunky: 6 or fewer wraps.
Substituting yarn

When a pattern names a specific brand, substitute within the same weight first. A DK cotton substitutes for another DK cotton with predictable results. A DK wool substitutes for DK cotton with a softer drape but the same dimensions. An aran substituted for a DK changes the finished size — the same pattern will be roughly 25% larger in aran than in DK.

Always swatch a substituted yarn against the pattern's gauge. Even within the same weight, different fibres have slightly different thicknesses; the swatch is the only way to confirm before starting the piece.
Yarn fibre and what it does
Cotton — smooth, structured, doesn't stretch. Used for dishcloths, bags, summer garments, amigurumi. Shows stitches clearly; the right choice for learning swatches.
Wool — warm, springy, takes blocking well. The classic blanket and garment fibre. Steam blocks beautifully.
Acrylic — machine-washable, lightweight, inexpensive. Used for blankets and children's items. Does not steam-block; use wet or spray blocking.
Bamboo / silk / linen — drape-heavy, slippery, summer-weight. Used for shawls and garments where drape matters more than structure.
Blends — combine the properties. Cotton-acrylic blends are washable and structured; wool-acrylic blends are warm and easy-care.
What to try next
